attrs.label: What is international SEO?
attrs.html:
What is international SEO?

International SEO makes sure the right version of your website ranks in each country and language you sell in. It covers how your site is structured, how its versions are linked, and what each market actually searches for.

  1. 1

    The right version for each searcher

    Language and country versions linked with hreflang, so a buyer in Dubai sees prices in dirhams and a buyer in Munich sees German.

  2. 2

    Research in every market

    People search differently in each country, even in the same language. Keywords are researched market by market, not translated.

  3. 3

    A structure Google understands

    Country domains, subfolders or subdomains, chosen for your business and set up so each version can rank.

attrs.label: Choosing the right site structure
attrs.html:
Choosing the right site structure

The first big decision in international SEO, and the hardest to change later. Answer three questions to see what we’d usually recommend.

Do you run a separate business or brand in each country?
Can you build content and links for each country’s site separately?
Does each country run on its own platform or tech team?

  • Recommended for you

    Country domains

    linea.co.uk · linea.ae · linea.de

    The strongest local signal, and separate sites for separate businesses.

    • Clear country targeting
    • Trusted by local buyers
    • Each site builds authority from zero
    • The most to run and maintain

  • Recommended for you

    Subfolders

    linea.example/en-gb/ · /ar-ae/ · /de-de/

    One domain, one set of links, with a folder per market. The right choice for most businesses.

    • All markets share your domain’s authority
    • One platform, one team
    • Needs careful hreflang and geo set-up
    • Less local feel than a country domain

  • Recommended for you

    Subdomains

    uk.linea.example · ae.linea.example

    Useful when each market runs on its own platform or is managed by a separate team.

    • Separate hosting and tech per market
    • Easy to hand to local teams
    • Authority is shared less than with subfolders
    • More set-up and tracking

attrs.label: Bringing your country sites together
attrs.html:
Bringing your country sites together

Many businesses grow market by market and end up with a different domain, subdomain or platform in each country. Each one fights for rankings on its own. We bring them together under one structure, without losing the traffic each site has earned.

  1. 01

    Audit every site

    Rankings, traffic, links and content for each domain, so nothing valuable is lost.

  2. 02

    Choose the target structure

    Usually one domain with a folder per market, sometimes keeping a country domain that earns its place.

  3. 03

    Map every URL

    A redirect map from every old page with traffic or links to its new home.

  4. 04

    Merge and clean up content

    Duplicates combined, the best version kept, gaps filled by native writers.

  5. 05

    Set up hreflang and geo signals

    Every market version linked, with local addresses, currencies and Search Console set up per folder.

  6. 06

    Launch and watch

    Redirects tested on launch day, then rankings and traffic tracked market by market for three months.

What you gain

  • All markets share one domain’s authority
  • One platform to run, update and secure
  • One brand and one set of analytics
  • Lower hosting, plugin and maintenance costs

Done badly, a consolidation can wipe out years of rankings. That’s why every old URL is mapped and tested before anything goes live. We check every version with a technical SEO audit before and after launch.

attrs.label: hreflang, done properly
attrs.html:
hreflang, done properly

hreflang tags tell Google which language and country each version is for. They’re the most common thing we fix on international sites, because one missing link breaks the whole set.

hreflang tagshtml
<!-- On every version of /dining-tables/ --><link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-gb" href="https://linea.example/en-gb/dining-tables/"><link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-us" href="https://linea.example/en-us/dining-tables/"><link rel="alternate" hreflang="ar-ae" href="https://linea.example/ar-ae/طاولات-طعام/"><link rel="alternate" hreflang="de-de" href="https://linea.example/de-de/esstische/"><link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href="https://linea.example/dining-tables/">

  • Missing return links

    Every version must link to every other. One missing link and Google ignores the pair, like the red line in the map.

  • Wrong codes

    “en-uk” instead of “en-gb”, or a country without a language. Invalid codes are skipped.

  • Pointing at redirects or noindexed pages

    hreflang must point to the final, indexable URL of each version.

  • Conflicts with canonicals

    Each version should be its own canonical, not point to the English page.

  • No x-default

    Without it, visitors from markets you don’t serve land on a random version.

attrs.label: Localisation, not translation
attrs.html:
Localisation, not translation

Translating your English pages word for word is the most common international SEO mistake. Even between the UK and the US, people use different words, currencies and payment options. SEO localisation adapts each page to the market.

UK page, copied to the US site

Oak dining tables from £499, made to order and delivered free to your flat. Choose from 12 finishes and pay in 3 instalments with Klarna.

“Flat”, pounds and Klarna: a US buyer leaves.

Localised for the US

Solid oak dining tables from $649, made to order with free shipping to your apartment or home. Choose from 12 finishes and pay over time with Affirm.

US words, dollars and a US payment option.

We already have trusted native writers and editors in each market. You get local-language content without finding, hiring or managing a writer yourself, and one team to brief for every country.

The nuances they get right

  • Tone and formality

    German buyers expect the formal “Sie” on most business sites; American readers expect a warmer, direct tone.

  • The words people search

    “Holiday” in the UK, “vacation” in the US. “Mobile” in Dubai, “cell phone” in Chicago. Native writers know which one ranks.

  • Prices, units and formats

    Currency, VAT, sizes in centimetres or inches, dates and phone formats, matched to each market.

  • Trust signals

    Local reviews, payment options, delivery promises and legal pages buyers in that country look for.

  • Culture and context

    Holidays, seasons, imagery and examples that make sense to the reader, and nothing that jars.

attrs.label: What goes wrong with international sites
attrs.html:
What goes wrong with international sites

These are the problems we find most often when a business has launched in new markets without an international SEO plan. Choose one to see how it happens and how we fix it.

Mistake 1 of 6

Redirecting by IP address

Sending every visitor to “their” country version sounds helpful. But Googlebot crawls mostly from US addresses, so it gets redirected to the US version every time and never sees the others. Those versions drop out of Google, and travellers or expats can’t reach the version they want.

How it happens

  • Geo-IP redirects added by a plugin, CDN rule or developer
  • Automatic redirects based on browser language
  • No way for a visitor to switch versions

How we fix it

  • Remove forced redirects; suggest the local version with a banner instead
  • Keep every version reachable by URL for people and Googlebot
  • Use hreflang to point each searcher to the right version
Request as Googlebothttp
$ curl -sI -A "Googlebot" https://linea.example/ar-ae/HTTP/2 302location: https://linea.example/en-us/Googlebot crawls mostly from the US, so it is sent to the US version every time and never sees /ar-ae/.

Mistake 2 of 6

Machine translation

Unedited machine translation misses local terms, gets tone wrong and often leaves titles, meta descriptions, image alt text and URLs untranslated. Searchers see English snippets on German results, trust drops, and Google can treat the pages as low-quality content.

How it happens

  • Whole sites run through a translation plugin with no review
  • Body text translated, but titles, meta and URLs left in English
  • Product names and units copied as they are

How we fix it

  • Native writers localise the key pages first
  • Titles, meta descriptions, alt text and URLs translated too
  • A second native speaker reviews before anything goes live

Mistake 3 of 6

Three identical English sites

Many businesses copy their UK pages to US and Australian versions and change little else. With no hreflang and no real differences, Google sees duplicates, picks one version to rank, and shows UK pages and prices to Australian searchers.

How it happens

  • Same text on every English version
  • Missing or broken hreflang between them
  • Canonicals pointing every version at the UK page

How we fix it

  • hreflang linking every English version both ways
  • Each version localised: spelling, terms, prices and delivery
  • Each version its own canonical

Search Console · URL Inspection

URLlinea.example/en-au/dining-tables/
Page indexingDuplicate, Google chose different canonical than user
User-declared canonical/en-au/dining-tables/
Google-selected canonical/en-gb/dining-tables/

Same text on the UK and Australian pages, no hreflang: Google shows the UK page in Australia.

Mistake 4 of 6

Mixed currencies and prices

Prices show in the wrong currency, or the price in the structured data doesn’t match the page. Google may show £ prices to US searchers, or drop the price and stock from your results altogether. Either way, people scroll past.

How it happens

  • One price field reused across all versions
  • Currency switched by JavaScript after the page loads
  • Product schema copied from the main store

How we fix it

  • Prices and currency set per version, in the HTML
  • Product and Offer schema with the right currency on every version
  • Merchant Center feeds per country, where you run Shopping ads

Price on the page vs price in Product schema

PageOn pageIn schemaCheck
/en-us/dining-tables/$649GBP 499Mismatch
/en-ae/dining-tables/AED 1,850GBP 499Mismatch
/de-de/esstische/549 €EUR 549OK

The theme prints the UK price into the structured data on every version, so Google shows £ prices to US and UAE searchers, or drops the rich result.

Mistake 5 of 6

One set of keywords for every market

Translating your English keyword list into other languages, or reusing UK keywords in the US, targets the wrong searches. Each market uses its own words for the same thing, and the search volumes can differ a hundredfold.

How it happens

  • Keyword lists translated, not researched
  • UK terms used on US and Australian pages
  • No research into the English searches people make in non-English markets

How we fix it

  • Keyword research in every market and language
  • Native writers check the terms locals actually use
  • Separate targets for local-language and English searches in the same market

US searches a month · same meaning, different words

Copying UK pages to the US site targets searches almost nobody in the US makes.

Mistake 6 of 6

No local signals

Google and buyers both look for proof that you really serve a country: a local address or phone number, local reviews, local payment and delivery options, legal pages and links from local sites. Without them, a country version looks like a translated copy of the main site.

How it happens

  • No local contact details on the country version
  • Reviews and case studies only from the home market
  • No local links, listings or press

How we fix it

  • Local contact details, delivery and payment options per market
  • Local reviews and proof on each version
  • Local link building and business listings

Local signals · linea.example/de-de/

  • Local address and phone number
  • Prices in the local currency
  • Reviews from local customers
  • Local legal pages (Impressum, VAT details)
  • Links from sites in the country
  • Search Console property for /de-de/

2 of 6: to Google and to German buyers, the page looks like a copy of the UK site.

items.question: What is international SEO?
items.answer: International SEO makes sure the right version of your website ranks in each country and language you sell in. It covers site structure, hreflang tags, localised content and market-by-market keyword research.

items.question: Should we use country domains, subfolders or subdomains?
items.answer: For most businesses, subfolders on one domain (for example /en-gb/ and /ar-ae/) are the best choice, because every market shares the same authority. Country domains suit separate businesses in each country; subdomains suit markets run on separate platforms.

items.question: What is hreflang and why does it matter?
items.answer: hreflang tags tell Google which language and country each version of a page is for, so it shows the right one to each searcher. Every version must link to every other, or Google ignores them.

items.question: Can we just translate our English site?
items.answer: Translation is a start, but people search differently in each market, even in the same language. We research keywords in each market and localise pages, including currencies, terms and examples.

items.question: What is SEO localisation?
items.answer: SEO localisation adapts content for a market: the words people search for, currency, units, payment options, examples and tone, not just the language.

items.question: Do you use AI to write content?
items.answer: No. We never write content with AI. Every page is written by a native-speaking writer and proofread by a second native speaker. We use AI only for research, and to learn what kind of content AI tools cite in each market, so our plans reflect how people search today.

items.question: Do you work in Arabic?
items.answer: Yes. Our team writes and builds in Arabic, including right-to-left layouts and research into both Arabic and English searches in Arabic-speaking markets.

items.question: How much do international SEO services cost?
items.answer: It depends on the number of markets and languages and how your site is built. Every plan is a fixed price, quoted after a free 30-minute call.

items.question: How long until a new market ranks?
items.answer: A new market version usually starts ranking for less competitive searches within two to three months of launch, and builds over six to twelve months.
